items.elements: Low hoots around 0.5 kHz, each with arched harmonics stacked up to about 2 kHz: a faint lone note at 0.3 s, then arched hoots at about 0.8, 1.15, 1.4, 1.9, 2.4, 2.8 and 3.05 s, the last one trailing off in a long downward slur that ends around 3.6 s. The hoots come in loose groups: one, a pair, one, one, then a pair that ends in the slur.
items.phrase: Who cooks, for you; who cooks for you-all
items.grounds: The eight low arched notes, grouped as a pickup, a pair, two singles and a closing pair, with the drawn-out falling slur at the end, gave me eight beats with a long falling last syllable; but the words themselves came from the well-known Barred Owl mnemonic 'who cooks for you, who cooks for you all', which I already knew, and I fitted it to the count rather than finding it in the picture.

items.elements: Clear pure whistles: one long, steady, very slightly falling tone at about 4.4 kHz from 0 to 2 s, then three shorter steady tones that step down, at about 4.5 kHz (2.3 to 2.9 s), about 4.0 kHz (3.1 to 3.6 s) and about 3.2 kHz (3.8 to 4.9 s, the longest of the three). Fainter chips and short sweeps from another bird sit behind them at 2 to 6 kHz.
items.grounds: One long held high tone followed by three level notes, each a step lower than the last, with the final one held, gave me a long opening vowel and three falling one-syllable words with the last one drawn out; I knew the 'Old Sam Peabody' and 'O sweet Canada' mnemonics, but this cut has no triplets, so I did not use them, though 'sweet' probably came from that memory.

items.elements: Two clean whistled notes: a first note at about 3.9 kHz drifting down to 3.6 kHz (0.25 to 0.63 s), a short gap, then a lower and slightly longer note held level at about 3.1 to 3.2 kHz (0.73 to 1.2 s), with a faint tail.
items.grounds: Two pure tones, the first higher and slightly falling and the second lower, level and longer, suggested a two-word greeting with the pitch dropping onto a held second word; I already knew the 'fee-bee' and 'hey, sweetie' renderings of this song, and that knowledge surely nudged me toward a greeting.

items.elements: A fast run of short slurred notes: two upslurs climbing to about 8 kHz (0.1 and 0.3 s), two downslurs from about 7 kHz (0.47 and 0.62 s), six small quick notes with a down-up shape around 3 to 5 kHz (about 0.75 to 1.5 s), then four loud, wide downstrokes from about 7 kHz to 4 kHz (1.65 to 2.17 s), and a final rising stroke (about 2.27 s).
items.phrase: Wee wee, slide down, tick tick tick tick tick tick, DROP DROP DROP DROP, up
items.grounds: The groups in the picture set the words: two rising notes, two falling notes, six small quick ones, four loud steep falls, and one last rise, so each word covers one element and the stress falls on the loud final four; I knew the 'sweet sweet sweet, I'm so sweet' mnemonic, but it did not fit this count and I did not use it.

items.elements: A varied, choppy phrase: a sharp broadband chip at 0.27 s, a long smooth rise from 2 to 4.5 kHz (0.5 to 0.72 s) ending in a short down-hook, a burst of buzzy broadband pulses (about 0.9 to 1.05 s), a falling slur from 3 to 2 kHz (1.07 to 1.2 s), a quick up-and-down stroke (about 1.3 s), a very sharp high upsweep to about 10 kHz (1.5 s), and a final short downstroke (1.57 s).
items.phrase: Snap! Rise-up, burr, down, quick, ping, drop
items.grounds: Each word copies the shape of one element: a hard click at the start, a long climb with a hook, a buzzy burst, a falling slur, a quick up-and-down, a high snap and a final drop; I knew the 'quick, give me a rain check' / 'pick-up-a-real-chick' mnemonics for this species, but I did not use them, since the words here come from the shapes.
